Decomposition-Indexed Classicality: An A/R/F Framework for Observer-Dependent Quantum Experience
Authors/Creators
Almon, Ricardo
(Producer)
Contributors
Producer:
Almon, Ricardo
Description
This work develops a quantitative framework for
observer-dependent classicality
in quantum mechanics based on three operational functionals:
Redundancy (R)
,
Accessibility (A)
, and
Observer Flow (F)
. The A/R/F framework distinguishes environmental redundancy from the effective redundancy usable by a specific observer, models accessibility through a noisy-threshold aperture function, and introduces a continuity measure governing an observer’s capacity to integrate records over time. Classicality becomes a
decomposition-indexed property
, not a global feature of the universal wavefunction.
Applied to
Wigner’s Friend
and
Frauchiger–Renner
, the framework dissolves paradoxes by showing that cross-agent inferences fail precisely in regimes where effective accessibility is low. The paper outlines experimental signatures, including observer-dependent classicality thresholds and flow-disruption tests, offering a route toward
empirical constraints on observer-relative quantum structure
.

The many different incarnations of nucleotide sequence (string) replicator models proposed recently are all attempts to explain on this basis how the genetic information transfer and the functional diversity of prebiotic replicator systems may have emerged, persisted and evolved into the first living cell. We have postulated three necessary conditions for an RNA World model system to be a dynamically feasible representation of prebiotic chemical evolution: (1) it must maintain and transfer a sufficient diversity of information reliably and indefinitely, (2) it must be ecologically stable and (3) it must be evolutionarily stable. Quantum Darwinism, Decoherence, and the Randomness of Quantum Jumps
Wojciech H. Zurek 1
1Theory Division, LANL, MS B213, Los Alamos, NM 87545
(Dated: June 1, 2014)
Tracing ﬂows of information in our quantum Universe explains why we see the world as classical.
Quantum principle of superposition decrees every combination of quantum states a legal quantum
state. This is at odds with our experience. Decoherence selects preferred pointer states that survive
interaction with the environment. They are localized and eﬀectively classical. They persist while
their superpositions decohere. Here we consider emergence of ‘the classical’ starting at a more
fundamental pre-decoherence level, tracing the origin of preferred pointer states and deducing their
probabilities from the core quantum postulates. We also explore role of the environment as medium
through which observers acquire information. This mode of information transfer leads to perception
of objective classical reality.
